claims.text: More than twenty different notions of algorithmic fairness have been proposed in recent years.
There is no clear agreement on which fairness definition to apply in each situation.
The same classification case can be evaluated as fair according to some definitions and unfair according to others.
The authors systematically collect and explain prominent definitions of fairness for algorithmic classification.
The authors demonstrate each fairness definition on a single unifying case-study.

evidence.description: The authors state there are 'more than twenty different notions of fairness proposed in the last few years.'
The paper notes that 'there is no clear agreement on which definition to apply in each situation.'
The paper's analysis 'intuitively explains why the same case can be considered fair according to some definitions and unfair according to others.'
The paper 'collects the most prominent definitions of fairness for the algorithmic classification problem, explains the rationale behind these definitions'.
The paper 'demonstrates each of them on a single unifying case-study.'

methodologies.name: Unifying Case Study Demonstration
methodologies.description: Application of multiple prominent algorithmic fairness definitions to a single unified case study for comparative analysis.

limitations.text: There is no clear agreement on which definition of fairness to apply in each situation.
Detailed differences between multiple definitions of fairness are difficult to grasp.
